# Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent

Xusen GUO xguo796@connect.hkust-gz.edu.cn    Xinxi YANG
xyang593@connect.hkust-gz.edu.cn    Mingxing PENG

hzhong638@connect.hkust-gz.edu.cn    Meixin ZHU meixin@seu.edu.cn    Hai
YANG cehyang@ust.hk organization=The Hong Kong University of Science and
Technology (Guangzhou), postcode=511453, state=Guangdong, country=China

postcode=211189, state=Nanjing, country=China organization=The Hong Kong

###### Abstract

Developing efficient traffic models is crucial for optimizing modern
transportation systems. However, current modeling approaches remain
labor-intensive and prone to human errors due to their dependence on
manual workflows. These processes typically involve extensive literature
reviews, formula tuning, and iterative testing, which often lead to
inefficiencies. To address this, we propose TR-Agent, an AI-powered
framework that autonomously develops and refines traffic models through
a closed-loop, iterative process. We structure the research pipeline
into four key stages—idea generation, theory formulation, theory
evaluation, and iterative optimization—and implement TR-Agent with four
corresponding modules. These modules collaborate to retrieve knowledge
from external sources, generate novel hypotheses, implement and debug
models, and evaluate their performance on evaluation datasets. Through
iteratively feedback and refinement, TR-Agent improves both modeling
efficiency and effectiveness. We validate the framework on three
representative traffic models: the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) for
car-following behavior, the MOBIL model for lane-changing, and the
Lighthill–Whitham–Richards (LWR) speed-density relationship for
macroscopic traffic flow modeling. Experimental results show substantial
performance gains over the original models. To assess the robustness and
generalizability of the improvements, we conduct additional evaluations
across multiple real-world datasets, demonstrating consistent
performance gains beyond the original development data. Furthermore,
TR-Agent produces interpretable explanations for each improvement,
enabling researchers to easily verify and extend its results. This makes
TR-Agent a valuable assistant for traffic modeling refinement and a
promising tool for broader applications in transportation research. To
facilitate future work, we have open-sourced our framework at
[https://github.com/Guoxs/TR-Agent](https://github.com/Guoxs/TR-Agent).

## 1 Introduction

Accurate and efficient traffic modeling plays a pivotal role in the
design and optimization of modern transportation systems. As
urbanization accelerates and traffic volumes grow, challenges such as
congestion management, road safety, and energy efficiency have become
increasingly urgent. Traffic models serve as the foundation for
addressing these challenges by providing a quantitative understanding of
vehicle behaviors and traffic dynamics. They are widely applied in
traffic simulation, infrastructure planning, real-time control, and
safety analysis. Applications include traffic flow
optimization ([Vallati et al., 2016](#bib.bib56); [Spiliopoulou et al.,
2017](#bib.bib48)), congestion prediction ([Pozanco et al.,
2021](#bib.bib41); [Chen et al., 2018](#bib.bib12)), collision risk
estimation ([Grushetsky et al., 2020](#bib.bib21); [Yannis et al.,
2017](#bib.bib61)), and emissions control ([Oskarbski et al.,
2021](#bib.bib38)). As transportation systems grow increasingly complex
and data-intensive, there is a pressing need for traffic models that are
efficient, adaptive, and interpretable, which calls for new tools and
methodologies to accelerate their development and refinement.

However, despite decades of development, the traditional workflow for
designing or improving traffic models remains largely manual and
inefficient ([Treiber and Kesting, 2013](#bib.bib53); [Brackstone and
McDonald, 1999](#bib.bib7)). Researchers often rely on extensive
literature reviews, domain expertise, and iterative trial-and-error to
propose and validate modifications to existing models ([Bhattacharyya
et al., 2021](#bib.bib6); [Chen et al., 2024b](#bib.bib10)). This
process is not only time-consuming and labor-intensive, but also limited
by individual researchers’ knowledge scope and cognitive capacity.
Moreover, refinements are typically driven by intuition or isolated
insights, which can lead to suboptimal designs or overlooked improvement
opportunities. As a result, many classical traffic models have remained
largely unchanged over time, despite well-known limitations in capturing
diverse traffic phenomena such as stop-and-go waves ([Stern et al.,
2018](#bib.bib49)), unstable following behavior ([Wang et al.,
2018](#bib.bib59)), or various lane-changing dynamics ([Li and Sun,
2017](#bib.bib29)). In particular, interpretable, rule-based models are
widely adopted due to their simplicity; however, they often struggle to
adapt to new traffic patterns or road scenarios without substantial
manual tuning ([Treiber et al., 2000](#bib.bib52)).

Recent breakthroughs in large language models (LLMs) ([Floridi and
Chiriatti, 2020](#bib.bib18); [Touvron et al., 2023](#bib.bib51);
[Anthropic, 2024](#bib.bib2); [OpenAI, 2023](#bib.bib37)) present a
compelling opportunity to rethink this workflow. LLMs have demonstrated
powerful capabilities in language understanding, reasoning, and code
generation ([Zhao et al., 2023](#bib.bib66)), enabling the rise of AI
agents—autonomous systems capable of performing complex tasks with
minimal human input. Leveraging techniques such as Chain-of-Thought
reasoning ([Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib60); [Yao et al.,
2022](#bib.bib62)), in-context learning ([Dai et al.,
2022](#bib.bib14)), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)  ([Lewis
et al., 2020](#bib.bib28)), and tool integration ([Schick et al.,
2024](#bib.bib46)), these agents can iteratively learn, adapt, and
refine strategies through feedback and experience. In fields ranging
from scientific discovery ([Qi et al., 2023](#bib.bib43); [Wang et al.,
2023a](#bib.bib57)), code synthesis ([Faldor et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)),
and data analysis ([Guo et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)) to chemistry ([Bran
et al., 2023](#bib.bib8)) and materials science ([Pyzer-Knapp et al.,
2022](#bib.bib42)), LLM-powered agents have already shown promise in
accelerating complex, research-intensive processes. However, their
application to physical model development (e.g., traffic models) remains
largely unexplored. Given the interpretability and real-world
significance of traffic models, applying autonomous agents to their
refinement offers a unique opportunity to advance transportation science
through a new, AI-driven paradigm.

Figure 1: Framework of the TR-Agent. TR-Agent consists of four
components: the Idea Generator, which retrieves knowledge from external
resources and generates novel ideas; the Code Generator, which
translates these ideas into new models; the Evaluator, which evaluates
the performance of the new models; and the Analyzer, which reviews the
experiment reports and provides feedback for the next iteration.

This work presents the Traffic Research Agent (TR-Agent), an AI-driven,
modular framework that autonomously refines interpretable traffic models
through an iterative process that mirrors human reasoning. As
illustrated in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent"),
TR-Agent consists of four interconnected modules: an Idea Generator that
proposes model refinements based on literature and feedback; a Code
Generator that translates ideas into executable models; an Evaluator
that quantitatively assesses performance using domain-specific metrics;
and an Analyzer that diagnoses failure cases and loops feedback back
into the improvement cycle. Rather than relying on end-to-end training
or opaque black-box methods, TR-Agent follows a structured and
explainable process: each model refinement is transparent, grounded in
domain knowledge, and documented with interpretable rationales. This
enables researchers to trace, verify, and further extend each
improvement, positioning TR-Agent not as a model replacement tool, but
as a collaborative assistant for interpretable model evolution.

To validate the framework, we apply TR-Agent to three canonical traffic
models: IDM (car-following), MOBIL (lane-changing), and LWR (macroscopic
flow). Extensive experiments demonstrate that TR-Agent can consistently
produce meaningful and generalizable improvements. We conduct additional
evaluations on a wide range of unseen real-world datasets, spanning
diverse traffic conditions, road types, and geographic locations. The
results confirm that the refined models not only outperform their
baselines across core metrics, but also maintain strong generalization
beyond the original data used in the refinement process. Furthermore,
visualizations and error pattern analyses indicate that the refinements
introduced by TR-Agent align well with empirical traffic patterns,
offering interpretable adjustments that enhance the model’s ability to
represent complex, real-world behaviors.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

- •
  Methodological Innovation: We introduce TR-Agent, the first autonomous
  LLM-based framework for traffic model refinement that integrates
  literature grounding, code generation, formal evaluation, and
  iterative optimization in a closed-loop workflow.
- •
  Interpretability and Traceability: TR-Agent produces model
  improvements that are structurally interpretable, verifiable, and
  explainable—facilitating human understanding, trust, and adoption.
- •
  Robust Generalization: Through extensive cross-dataset experiments, we
  demonstrate that TR-Agent-refined models exhibit strong performance
  and generalizability across heterogeneous real-world traffic
  scenarios, confirming the practical utility of our framework.
- •
  Model-Agnostic and Transferable Design: TR-Agent is not limited to a
  specific traffic model; it can be applied to a variety of rule-based
  models and easily adapted to other domains involving interpretable
  mathematical modeling.

While TR-Agent greatly enhances the efficiency and scalability of model
development, it is not designed to replace human researchers. Rather, it
functions as a collaborative assistant, which augments human expertise
with automated, data-driven reasoning to accelerate model iteration and
inspire new directions. By enabling the rapid generation of verifiable
and explainable candidate solutions, TR-Agent streamlines the refinement
process and significantly reduces the time and effort required for model
development. We believe this framework offers a promising foundation for
integrating AI-guided reasoning into scientific modeling, not only in
transportation, but also in other domains where interpretability and
formal structure are critical.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 LLMs for Scientific Research

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated
substantial potential in automating scientific research workflows.
Beyond language understanding, LLMs now offer powerful capabilities in
synthesis, reasoning, and structured generation, enabling new paradigms
in AI-assisted discovery. In the context of machine learning and AI
research, studies such as ([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)) and ([Lu
et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)) show how LLMs can generate novel algorithms,
critique research ideas, and support experimental design. Similarly,
([Liang et al., 2024](#bib.bib30)) reveal that LLMs can provide
peer-review-quality comments on scientific manuscripts, indicating their
potential as research collaborators. Systems like ResearchAgent ([Baek
et al., 2024](#bib.bib3)) and SciMon ([Wang et al., 2023b](#bib.bib58))
have demonstrated the ability of LLMs to autonomously identify gaps in
the literature and propose new directions. However, these tools
typically stop at ideation and do not execute or validate the proposed
models.

LLMs have also been explored for structured reasoning and optimization.
Works like ([Zhang et al., 2023](#bib.bib65); [Lange et al.,
2024](#bib.bib27)) apply LLMs to black-box optimization and
multi-objective search, while ([Chen et al., 2024a](#bib.bib9)) show
their utility in evolving neural architectures through prompt-based
evolution. Despite these successes, current efforts are often
constrained to neural architectures or software-related domains and
rarely target interpretable, rule-based physical models. Our work
bridges this gap by demonstrating how LLMs can not only assist with
ideation but autonomously develop and refine classical traffic models in
an interpretable and verifiable manner.

### 2.2 AI Agents for Autonomous Innovation

The emergence of LLM-powered agents has introduced new opportunities for
automating the entire research and development pipeline. ReAct ([Yao
et al., 2022](#bib.bib62)) and Reflexion ([Shinn et al.,
2024](#bib.bib47)) show that agents equipped with memory and reasoning
can iteratively solve tasks by learning from their failures. These
principles have been widely adopted in autonomous agents for programming
(e.g., Codex ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib11)), Copilot ([Svyatkovskiy
et al., 2020](#bib.bib50))) and data analysis ([Guo et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22); [Hollmann et al., 2024](#bib.bib23)), where agents
can write, test, and refine code in closed-loop workflows. Beyond
software domains, AI agents have begun to contribute to experimental
sciences. For instance, ChemCrow ([Bran et al., 2023](#bib.bib8))
designs and executes chemical experiments, and agents like those
proposed by ([Pyzer-Knapp et al., 2022](#bib.bib42); [Merchant et al.,
2023](#bib.bib34)) assist in materials discovery. These applications
demonstrate the feasibility of using autonomous agents in real-world,
domain-specific research tasks.

Despite these advances, relatively little work explores the use of AI
agents in the development of interpretable, rule-based physical models
such as those used in transportation systems. Most agents focus on
optimizing parameters or accelerating trial-and-error cycles, rather
than generating novel structural improvements. TR-Agent addresses this
gap by enabling end-to-end refinement of traffic models through a
self-improving agent framework that integrates idea generation, model
coding, formal evaluation, and feedback-driven iteration. Unlike
existing agents, TR-Agent operates directly on domain-relevant
mathematical formulations and produces transparent, interpretable
modifications—paving the way for more intelligent, generalizable
modeling pipelines in traffic science and beyond.

Figure 2: Illustration of the Idea Generator Module. The Idea Generation
Prompt is used only in the first iteration to generate initial ideas for
each trial, after which the Idea Refinement Prompt is employed in
subsequent iterations to continuously refine the ideas.

## 3 Methodology

Our proposed TR-Agent is designed as an AI-driven system capable of
autonomously generating, refining, and evaluating traffic models. As
illustrated in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent"),
the framework comprises four core components: the Idea Generator, Code
Generator, Evaluator, and Analyzer. Working in concert, these modules
form a closed-loop system that mimics the typical human research
workflow. The process begins with the Idea Generator, which retrieves
domain knowledge from academic literature and online sources and uses
prompt-guided reasoning to propose model improvements. These suggestions
are passed to the Code Generator, which translates the ideas into
executable code. The resulting model is then evaluated by the Evaluator
using predefined datasets and metrics. The evaluation results are
reviewed by the Analyzer, which determines whether the proposed
modifications meet the performance threshold. If successful, the
improvement is accepted and documented; otherwise, the Analyzer provides
structured feedback to guide the next iteration. This loop continues
until a satisfactory model refinement is achieved.

In the following sections, we describe the design and implementation
details of each component in the TR-Agent framework.

### 3.1 Idea Generator

The Idea Generator is the starting point of the TR-Agent framework,
tasked with proposing mathematically grounded refinements to traffic
models by leveraging both the internal capabilities of large language
models and external domain knowledge. As illustrated in
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 AI Agents for Autonomous Innovation ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent"),
this module operates in two stages: initial idea generation and
iterative refinement.

In the first iteration, the Idea Generation Prompt is used to guide the
LLM in understanding the mathematical structure of the target model,
identifying its potential deficiencies, and proposing improvements. To
enrich the LLM’s context, we adopt a Retrieval-Augmented Generation
(RAG) mechanism ([Lewis et al., 2020](#bib.bib28)), enabling access to
both offline academic literature and online traffic modeling resources.
This ensures that the generated ideas are informed by a wide range of
domain-relevant knowledge.

If the generated idea fails to meet the expected performance after
implementation and evaluation, the process enters an iterative
refinement loop. In this stage, the Analyzer module provides structured
feedback, including diagnoses of failure cases and suggestions for
further improvement. These are compiled into a follow-up Idea Refinement
Prompt, which updates the LLM with contextualized insights from the
previous trial. This prompt asks the LLM to revise its original idea,
formulate a more targeted solution, or retrieve additional supporting
knowledge as needed.

By continuously cycling through this loop, the Idea Generator produces
increasingly refined, interpretable, and theoretically plausible
improvements. This design not only automates the ideation process but
also mimics how human researchers iteratively enhance models based on
both theoretical reasoning and empirical feedback.

### 3.2 Code Generator

Figure 3: Illustration of the Code Generator Module. The diagram depicts
the iterative process of transforming novel ideas into executable model
functions. Initially, the rough code for the improved model is generated
using the Code Generation Prompt. Then, an iterative debugging process
follows, guided by the Code Refinement Prompt, to refine the code and
ensure it is executable.

The Code Generator module is designed to transform conceptual
improvement ideas into executable traffic model functions. As
illustrated in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Code Generator ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent"),
it leverages the programming capabilities of large language models
(LLMs) to synthesize and iteratively refine code based on high-level
structural ideas provided by the Idea Generator.

The process begins with a Code Generation Prompt, which presents the LLM
with a partially filled Python function template (e.g.,
Improved\_\<model_name\>). This template includes pre-defined input
parameters (such as spacing, velocity, relative speed) and expected
output formats (e.g., acceleration). Along with this, the prompt also
includes the natural language description of the proposed improvement
and model-specific coding constraints. Guided by this prompt, the LLM
generates an initial version of the implementation.

To ensure correctness and feasibility, the generated function is passed
through an iterative refinement loop. This loop is structured as
follows:

- •
  Unit Testing: The initial version of the function is tested using a
  set of unit test cases that verify whether the code executes correctly
  on representative inputs and produces outputs in the expected format
  and range.
- •
  Automated Debugging: If errors occur, such as runtime exceptions,
  undefined variables, or format mismatches, they are captured and
  compiled into a Code Refinement Prompt. This prompt, along with
  specific debugging instructions, is then fed back to the LLM to
  produce a revised version of the code.
- •
  Refinement Iteration: This process continues until a valid function is
  produced that passes all unit tests and satisfies basic interface and
  behavioral consistency. While the correctness of the outputs is not
  strictly verified at this stage, successful execution ensures the
  function can be further evaluated in downstream tasks.

The design of this module prioritizes structural feasibility and
execution correctness, providing a solid foundation for further
validation by the Evaluator module. While deeper semantic verification
such as performance accuracy or behavioral fidelity is conducted in
later stages, the Code Generator ensures that novel ideas are reliably
translated into executable model code, facilitating smooth integration
within the TR-Agent pipeline.

Figure 4: Left: Idea Refinement Prompt is used in the iteration process
of the Idea Generator, guiding the enhancement of proposed ideas based
on previous iteration feedback from the Analyzer. Right: Code Refinement
Prompt that assists in debugging and improving the source code of a new
model by utilizing error messages and adhering to specific coding
guidelines.

### 3.3 Evaluator

The Evaluator module is responsible for systematically assessing the
performance of the traffic model generated by the Code Generator. Unlike
other components, it does not rely on LLMs and instead follows a
deterministic, programmatic pipeline to ensure objective and
reproducible evaluation.

Once an executable model function is generated, the Evaluator loads the
designated test dataset and executes the model across all data samples.
During execution, the system collects both intermediate and final
outputs, such as predicted vehicle spacing, lane-change decisions, or
traffic speed–density relationships, depending on the specific modeling
task. These outputs are then compared with ground-truth labels or
reference trajectories to compute the corresponding evaluation metrics.

We adopt task-specific metrics to assess different types of models. For
car-following models, we report spacing MAE under different driving
scenarios for tracking accuracy. Other metrics can also be applied such
as jerk (for comfort), and time-to-collision (for safety). For
lane-changing models, we use precision, recall, and F1 score to evaluate
decision quality. For traffic flow models, we measure MAE under
different density regimes to capture behavior across traffic conditions.

To ensure transparency and traceability, the Evaluator generates a
structured log file that records metric values and evaluation summaries.
These logs are automatically parsed and formatted into performance
reports, which are then passed to the Analyzer for further reasoning.
Scenario-based breakdowns (e.g., low/high density or different driver
behaviors) are supported, allowing fine-grained performance analysis.

The Evaluator is highly customizable. By adjusting the evaluation
dataset or metric configuration, users can guide TR-Agent to optimize
toward different modeling goals, such as improving fuel efficiency,
enhancing safety, or reducing congestion. This modularity allows the
framework to generalize across tasks and domains, while remaining
aligned with specific application objectives.

### 3.4 Analyzer

Figure 5: Illustration of the Analyzer Module. The module analyzes
experiment reports generated during trials, using two distinct prompts
to guide its analysis: one for successful trials and another for failed
trials. The System Prompt serves as the guiding instruction, asking the
Analyzer to review trial logs, assess whether the performance criteria
were met, and provide suggestions for further improvements if needed.

Figure 6: Top: Successful Trail Analysis Prompt. This prompt is used
when the latest trial meets performance requirements. It provides
baseline model information and the last iteration’s experiment log, with
instructions to analyze the reasons behind the observed improvements.
Bottom: Failed Trail Analysis Prompt. This prompt is used when the
latest trial fails to meet performance requirements. It includes
baseline model information and logs from the last three improved
iterations, along with guidelines for analyzing the causes of low
performance and suggesting further improvements.

The Analyzer module is responsible for interpreting the outcomes of each
model refinement trial and providing actionable feedback to guide
subsequent iterations. It serves as a reasoning engine that evaluates
the effectiveness of the modified model, determines whether the
predefined performance threshold has been met, and formulates
suggestions accordingly. The analysis process is guided by a structured
System Prompt and two specialized prompts for success and failure
scenarios, as depicted in
Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.4 Analyzer ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent").

Once the Evaluator has assessed the model and generated a log report,
the Analyzer loads this log and parses key segments: the baseline model
performance and the experiment history from recent iterations. The
module then performs one of the following based on the evaluation
result:

- •
  Successful Trial: If the model achieves the desired performance
  improvement, the Analyzer uses the Successful Trial Analysis Prompt
  (top of
  Figure [6](#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 3.4 Analyzer ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent"))
  to identify and summarize the key changes responsible for the success.
  This includes a concise analysis of the model’s structural differences
  and how they contribute to improved behavior, which is then logged for
  human inspection and transparency.
- •
  Failed Trial: If the improvement threshold is not met, the module
  engages the Failed Trial Analysis Prompt (bottom of
  Figure [6](#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 3.4 Analyzer ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent")).
  This prompt includes the baseline log and the latest three improved
  iterations’ logs. The Analyzer is instructed to (1) diagnose failure
  causes and (2) propose concrete, mathematically grounded suggestions
  for the next iteration. Importantly, the prompt discourages trivial or
  generic suggestions (e.g., using machine learning or parameter tuning)
  and ensures all feedback remains within the domain of interpretable,
  rule-based modeling.

To maintain scientific rigor, the module also formulates a set of
targeted exploratory questions designed to deepen model understanding
and guide the next round of improvement. These questions aim to uncover
overlooked deficiencies, validate model assumptions, and stimulate
theory-driven enhancements. The logic underpinning this process is
implemented via a structured log parser, which isolates the baseline
model summary, evaluates iteration outcomes, and detects improvements
based on performance metrics. This ensures that any observed
improvements are systematically tracked, interpretable, and not a result
of random variations in code generation.

In essence, the Analyzer acts as a reflective engine within TR-Agent,
transforming raw performance data into structured insights and
iteratively refining model development based on empirical outcomes and
domain-relevant reasoning.

## 4 Background of Traffic Models

In this section, we introduce the background of the traffic models we
aim to improve. We selected three representative traffic models for
experiments to demonstrate the versatility and effectiveness of our
automatic research framework: IDM car-following model ([Treiber et al.,
2000](#bib.bib52)), MOBIL lane-changing model ([Kesting et al.,
2007](#bib.bib25)), and LWR traffic flow model ([Lighthill and Whitham,
1955](#bib.bib31); [Richards, 1956](#bib.bib44)). The rationale behind
choosing these models is twofold: first, they are well-known and widely
used in traffic research, representing different aspects of traffic
dynamics; and second, their simplicity and structure make them feasible
for iterative improvement, allowing TR-Agent to demonstrate its
optimization capabilities effectively.

#### 4.0.1 IDM Car-Following Model

The Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) is a car-following model developed to
simulate realistic driving behavior and traffic flow dynamics. The IDM
aims to describe how individual vehicles adapt their acceleration in
response to the surrounding traffic environment. It is widely used in
traffic engineering and transportation research due to its simplicity,
robustness, and ease of reproduction. The IDM is based on the principle
that a driver strives to maintain a safe and comfortable distance from
the leading vehicle while trying to reach a desired speed. The following
equation determines the acceleration $`a`$ of the following vehicle:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
a=a_{max}\left[1-\left(\frac{v}{v_{0}}\right)^{\delta}-\left(\frac{s^{*}(v,\Delta v)}{s}\right)^{2}\right]
``` |  | (1) |

where $`a_{max}`$ is the maximum acceleration, $`v`$ is the current
speed of the following vehicle, $`v_{0}`$ is the desired speed,
$`\delta`$ is the acceleration exponent, $`s`$ is the current gap to the
leading vehicle, and $`\Delta v`$ is the speed difference between the
following vehicle and leading vehicle. $`s^{*}(v,\Delta v)`$ is the
desired minimum gap, defined as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s^{*}(v,\Delta v)=s_{0}+\max\left(0,vT+\frac{v\Delta v}{2\sqrt{a_{max}b}}\right)
``` |  | (2) |

Here, $`s_{0}`$ is the minimum gap, $`T`$ is the desired time headway,
and $`b`$ is the comfortable deceleration. The IDM captures both
acceleration and deceleration behaviors, making it a robust model for
analyzing traffic dynamics and vehicle interactions.

#### 4.0.2 MOBIL Lane-Changing Model

The Minimizing Overall Braking Induced by Lane Changes (MOBIL) model is
a widely used decision-making framework in traffic simulation,
particularly for lane-changing behavior on multi-lane roads. Developed
to complement longitudinal driving models, such as IDM, MOBIL provides a
rule-based approach to lane changing by considering both the safety and
utility of the maneuver. The model evaluates whether a lane change
benefits the driver and the surrounding traffic, balancing the need to
minimize the braking of neighboring vehicles while maximizing individual
progress. According to MOBIL, the decision to change lanes is governed
by the following incentive criterion:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tilde{a}_{c}-a_{c}+p\left(\tilde{a}_{n}-a_{n}+\tilde{a}_{o}-a_{o}\right)>\Delta a_{th}
``` |  | (3) |

Here, $`\tilde{a}_{c}`$ is the new acceleration for the subject vehicle
after the lane change and $`a_{c}`$ is the current acceleration. The
terms $`\tilde{a}_{n}-a_{n}`$ and $`\tilde{a}_{o}-a_{o}`$ represent the
acceleration changes for the new and old followers, respectively. The
politeness factor $`p`$ adjusts the influence of these neighbors, while
$`\Delta a_{th}`$ is a threshold that prevents marginal lane changes. A
lane change is executed if the gain in the subject vehicle’s
acceleration outweighs the combined disadvantages to the new and old
followers, considering both personal benefit and overall traffic impact.

#### 4.0.3 LWR Traffic Flow Model

The Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) model was developed independently
by Lighthill and Whitham in 1955 ([Lighthill and Whitham,
1955](#bib.bib31)) and Richards in 1956 ([Richards, 1956](#bib.bib44)).
It describes traffic flow using the continuity equation, capturing the
conservation of vehicles, and an equilibrium speed-density relationship.
In this framework, the model assumes that traffic flow is always in a
state of equilibrium, meaning that the speed and density of vehicles at
any given point are instantly adjusted to maintain this balance.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{\partial q(x,t)}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial\rho(x,t)}{\partial t}=0
``` |  | (4) |

The continuity equation is presented at
Eq. [4](#S4.E4 "In 4.0.3 LWR Traffic Flow Model ‣ 4 Background of Traffic Models ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent"),
where $`q(x,t)`$ represents the traffic flow (vehicles per unit time),
and $`\rho(x,t)`$ denotes the traffic density (vehicles per unit length)
at position $`x`$ and time $`t`$. Another key component of the LWR model
is the relationship between traffic density $`\rho`$ and velocity $`v`$,
often modeled using the Greenshields fundamental diagram. This
relationship is given by:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{cases}q(\rho)=\rho v_{f}\left(1-\frac{\rho}{\rho_{m}}\right)\\
v(\rho)=v_{f}\left(1-\frac{\rho}{\rho_{m}}\right)\end{cases}
``` |  | (5) |

In this formulation, $`v_{f}`$ represents the free-flow speed, which is
the speed of vehicles when there is no congestion, and $`\rho_{m}`$
denotes the maximum traffic density, also known as jam density, where
vehicles are bumper-to-bumper. In our experiment, we mainly try to
improve the equation for $`v(\rho)`$ that describes how vehicle speed
decreases linearly with increasing traffic density using our TR-Agent.

## 5 Experimental Results

We validate the effectiveness and generalizability of TR-Agent across
three classic traffic modeling tasks: car-following (IDM), lane-changing
(MOBIL), and macroscopic traffic flow (LWR). For each task, we present a
representative improvement trajectory that illustrates how TR-Agent
iteratively refines interpretable model formulations based on feedback.
The complete logs of these iterative improvements can be found in
supplementary materials, and more improvement examples can be found in
our open-source repository on github. In addition to performance
metrics, we include generalization studies across diverse real-world
datasets and visualize error patterns to assess robustness and
interpretability. Our goal is not to develop new models themselves, but
to demonstrate that TR-Agent can serve as an effective assistant in
traffic model refinement by producing explainable, verifiable
improvements that generalize well across diverse scenarios.

The rest of this section is organized as follows. Section 5.1 presents
results on the IDM car-following model, including iterative
improvements, scenario-specific evaluation, and cross-dataset
generalization. Section 5.2 details the refinement of the MOBIL
lane-changing model and compares it against several baseline approaches.
Section 5.3 focuses on the macroscopic LWR flow model and illustrates
how TR-Agent captures nonlinear traffic dynamics. Finally, Section 5.4
and 5.5 provide additional analyses, including the role of literature
retrieval and performance trends over multiple iterations.

### 5.1 Improvement for IDM Car-Following Model

#### 5.1.1 Settings for Model Evaluation

We collected a dataset with 7960 car-following events on urban
expressways in Shanghai ([Zhu et al., 2018](#bib.bib67)) to evaluate the
performance of the TR-Agent-refined models. Each event in the dataset is
represented by an $`N\times 4`$ matrix, where $`N`$ denotes the time
steps, and the four columns correspond to spacing $`s`$, following
vehicle speed $`v`$, leading vehicle speed $`v_{l}`$, and the relative
speed $`\Delta v`$ between the following and leading vehicles,
respectively. The sampling frequency for these events is 10 Hz, with
each event lasting over 15 seconds, ensuring $`N>150`$ and thus
maintaining the completeness and uniqueness of the following events. As
the IDM requires hyper-parameter optimization, we need to calibrate the
model’s hyper-parameters to ensure a fair comparison of its performance.
Specifically, we randomly selected 20% of the following events to form
the calibration dataset, while the remaining 80% constituted the
validation dataset. We utilized genetic algorithms ([Mirjalili and
Mirjalili, 2019](#bib.bib35)) for hyper-parameter tuning, and use the
Mean Absolute Error (MAE) as the objective function to minimize the
discrepancy between simulated and observed spacing. The MAE is defined
as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
MAE=\frac{1}{MN}\sum^{M}_{i=1}\sum^{N}_{j=1}\left|s^{simulated}_{ij}-s^{observed}_{ij}\right|
``` |  | (6) |

where $`M`$ represents the number of following events, $`N`$ denotes the
number of time steps within each event, $`s^{simulated}_{ij}`$ is the
simulated vehicle spacing for the $`i`$-th event at the $`j`$-th time
step, and $`s^{observed}_{ij}`$ is the corresponding observed ground
truth.

To evaluate the model’s performance across different stages of the car
following process, we classified the data points in each event into four
categories: ”Free driving,” ”Following,” ”closing In,” and ”Emergency
braking,” based on the Wiedemann-99 model ([Aghabayk et al.,
2013](#bib.bib1)). Statistical analysis revealed that these four
categories represent 39.70%, 15.79%, 31.56%, and 12.95% of the data
points, indicating a relatively balanced sampling distribution. During
the evaluation phase, we report the overall MAE and the MAE for each
stage. These scenario-based performance evaluations allow for an
in-depth analysis of the model’s strengths and weaknesses across
different stages of car-following, enabling TR-Agent to provide more
targeted improvement suggestions.

Figure 7: The improvement process of IDM car-following model. We
selected two representative intermediate results along with the baseline
information and final improvement outcome for demonstration. Here
$`a_{max}`$ is the maximum acceleration, $`v`$ is the speed of the
target vehicle, $`v_{0}`$ is the desired speed, $`\delta`$ is the
acceleration exponent, $`s`$ is the spacing to the leading vehicle,
$`s_{0}`$ is the minimum spacing, $`T`$ is the desired time headway,
$`b`$ is the comfortable deceleration, and $`\Delta v`$ is the speed
difference between the target vehicle and leading vehicle. $`\beta`$ is
a newly introduced parameter in the model improvement process, with its
specific meaning determined by the corresponding improvement formula.

#### 5.1.2 Improvement Case Study

To showcase TR-Agent’s refinement capabilities, we selected a
representative IDM improvement case and visualized its full iterative
trajectory in
Figure [7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 5.1.1 Settings for Model Evaluation ‣ 5.1 Improvement for IDM Car-Following Model ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent").
The experiment report records each iteration’s code, evaluation results,
deficiency analysis, and suggested improvements. For clarity, we present
the baseline model, two intermediate iterations, and the final improved
version. Python functions are converted into mathematical expressions,
and textual annotations summarize key insights. The target improvement
threshold was set at 25%, with a maximum of 10 iterations per trial.

The baseline IDM showed relatively high errors in the ”Following” and
”Closing in” scenarios, with an overall MAE of 4.385. TR-Agent
identified that the squared term in the acceleration formula made the
model overly sensitive to spacing changes, leading to abrupt
deceleration or acceleration. In the first iteration (V1), it proposed a
smoothing mechanism using a sigmoid function to mitigate overreactions,
resulting in a 14.35% MAE improvement, especially under unstable
conditions. Building on this, the second iteration (V2) introduced
scenario-specific logic based on the sign of the spacing deviation,
triggering different acceleration responses for “too close” and
“comfortable” regimes. This hybrid design further improved performance
to 18.49%. Still short of the target, TR-Agent continued refining the
model. In the final iteration, it proposed three changes: replacing the
sigmoid with a bounded hyperbolic tangent function for smoother
deceleration, introducing dynamic weight adjustment based on real-time
relative speed, and adding a scenario detection mechanism. These
collectively enabled the model to adapt its behavior more flexibly and
robustly across diverse traffic conditions, ultimately achieving a
26.11% improvement.

This case study highlights TR-Agent’s ability to perform iterative,
interpretable model development, mimicking a domain expert by
systematically diagnosing weaknesses, applying targeted changes, and
validating their effectiveness. Each refinement is transparent and
traceable, reinforcing the agent’s value as an assistive tool in
scientific model development.

real-world test datasets from the benchmark study ([Chen et al.,
2023](#bib.bib13)). The number in parentheses indicates the number of

To assess the generalization ability of the refined IDM model, we
evaluate its performance across six diverse real-world datasets from the
FollowNet benchmark ([Chen et al., 2023](#bib.bib13)), including urban,
highway, and naturalistic driving environments: Lyft, NGSIM, SPMD1,
SPMD2, Waymo, and HighD. We compare five models: the baseline IDM, the
TR-Agent-refined IDM, and three classical baselines: Optimal Velocity
Model (OVM) ([Bando et al., 1995](#bib.bib5); [Bando et al.,
1998](#bib.bib4)), Full Velocity Difference Model (FVD) ([Gong et al.,
2008](#bib.bib20)), and Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) ([Kim et al.,
2012](#bib.bib26)). Evaluation is conducted using three metrics that
jointly reflect tracking precision (Spacing MAE), comfort (Jerk), and
safety (Time-to-Collision, TTC).

As shown in
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.1.3 Generalization Studies ‣ 5.1 Improvement for IDM Car-Following Model ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent"),
the TR-Agent-refined IDM achieves consistent performance improvements
over the original IDM across all datasets. On Lyft, the spacing MAE is
reduced by over 38% (from 45.61 m to 28.22 m), and on HighD, the TTC
increases dramatically from 313.9 s to 3575.44 s, suggesting
significantly enhanced safety. On average, the refined IDM demonstrates
not only better precision but also more stable longitudinal control,
with jerk values that remain within acceptable limits for comfort in
most cases. Compared to the classical models, the TR-Agent-refined IDM
offers a balanced trade-off. While FVD achieves excellent TTC in some
scenarios, it suffers from very high jerk (e.g., 5.6 m/s³ on Lyft),
indicating unstable acceleration. OVM maintains low jerk but compromises
safety (e.g., TTC of 96.73 s on NGSIM), and ACC shows moderate
performance across metrics but fails on datasets with complex traffic
dynamics (e.g., high spacing MAE on SPMD1 and SPMD2). In contrast,
TR-Agent’s refined model avoids extreme trade-offs and maintains robust,
interpretable performance across all conditions.

In order to better illustrate the error distributions of different
models across datasets,
Figure [8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.1.3 Generalization Studies ‣ 5.1 Improvement for IDM Car-Following Model ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent")
presents the spacing and speed MAE distributions for five representative
models on the Waymo and HighD datasets. The violin plots reveal both the
central tendency and the variability of each model’s prediction errors.
Across both datasets and evaluation metrics, the TR-Agent-refined IDM
achieves performance that is comparable to or better than the original
IDM. This is particularly evident in the spacing MAE on the HighD
dataset, where the refined model exhibits a more concentrated error
distribution with consistently lower values. Compared to other baseline
models, the refined model also demonstrates competitive performance.
Although it slightly underperforms FVD, which achieves the lowest
overall spacing errors, it clearly outperforms OVM and is generally
comparable to ACC. These results indicate that the TR-Agent refinement
improves both the accuracy and robustness of traditional car-following
models across diverse traffic scenarios.

These results collectively confirm that TR-Agent does not overfit to a
single dataset or scenario. Instead, the framework produces
generalizable improvements that transfer well across diverse traffic
environments, from dense urban settings (NGSIM) to naturalistic highway
data (HighD, SPMD), and from noisy onboard sensors (Waymo) to
fixed-point loop detectors (Lyft). Such cross-domain robustness
demonstrates the practical utility of our framework for real-world
traffic modeling and simulation.

### 5.2 Improvement for MOBIL Lane-Changing Model

#### 5.2.1 Settings for Model Evaluation

In this experiment, we evaluate the performance of the TR-Agent-refined
lane-changing model using the NGSIM I-80 trajectory dataset ([U.S.
Department of Transportation Federal Highway Administration,
2016](#bib.bib55)), which provides high-resolution, real-world vehicle
trajectory data including positions, speeds, and accelerations. For our
analysis, we identified lane change events and extracted data from the
three seconds preceding each lane change (at 10 Hz sampling rate) as
positive samples, representing instances immediately leading up to a
lane change. To construct a balanced classification dataset, we then
selected an equal number of non-lane-changing samples from the remaining
trajectories, focusing on scenes where a lane change did not occur and
was also not appropriate (e.g., due to lack of incentive or safety
conditions).

We evaluate model performance using the F1 score, which balances
precision and recall in binary classification, and also report
precision, recall, and specificity to provide a more comprehensive view
of predictive quality. The mathematical formulas for these metrics are
as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}\quad\text{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}\quad\text{Specificity}=\frac{TN}{TN+FP}
``` |  | (7) |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{F1 Score}=2\times\frac{\text{Precision}\times\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}}
``` |  | (8) |

Here, $`TP`$, $`TN`$, $`FP`$, and $`FN`$ denote true positives, true
negatives, false positives, and false negatives, respectively. The F1
score balances the precision and recall, providing a nuanced measure of
model performance. Precision indicates how many of the predicted
positive cases were actually correct, recall measures the model’s
ability to correctly identify positive cases, and specificity measures
the ability to correctly identify negative cases. These metrics
collectively provide a detailed evaluation of the model’s effectiveness
in predicting lane changes.

#### 5.2.2 Improvement Case Study

Figure 9: The improvement process of the MOBIL lane-changing model. We
selected two representative intermediate results along with the final
improvement outcome for demonstration. Here $`a_{c}`$, $`a_{n}`$,
$`a_{o}`$ and $`\tilde{a}_{c}`$, $`\tilde{a}_{n}`$, $`\tilde{a}_{o}`$
are the accelerations for the subject vehicle, old follower, and new
follower before and after the lane change events. $`p`$ is the
politeness factor, $`\Delta a_{th}`$ is a threshold that prevents
marginal lane changes, $`b_{safe}`$ is the safety-related boundary
constraint parameter. $`s_{tf}`$ and $`s_{tr}`$ are the relative
distances to the target lane’s front and rear vehicles.

Similar to the IDM example, we illustrate TR-Agent’s iterative
refinement process for the MOBIL lane-changing model in
Figure [9](#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 5.2.2 Improvement Case Study ‣ 5.2 Improvement for MOBIL Lane-Changing Model ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent").
To ensure clarity, we present the baseline, two intermediate iterations,
and the final improved model. A minimum performance improvement
threshold of 50% was applied, with hyperparameter calibration performed
using a genetic algorithm.

The baseline MOBIL model bases its decisions on a lane-changing
incentive function and a safety constraint
(Eq. [3](#S4.E3 "In 4.0.2 MOBIL Lane-Changing Model ‣ 4 Background of Traffic Models ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent")).
On our evaluation dataset, it exhibited weak predictive capability, with
a precision of 0.552, a recall of 0.215, and an F1 score of just 0.310.
TR-Agent identified several deficiencies, including overly simplistic
safety criteria, limited context awareness, and a short-sighted focus on
immediate gains. Its initial suggestions included strengthening the
safety logic, integrating cooperative reasoning (e.g., game theory), and
adopting dynamic decision thresholds.

The first refinement (V1) focused on modifying the safety condition.
Rather than using acceleration-based thresholds for the new follower
($`\tilde{a}_{n}`$), TR-Agent proposed a constraint based on relative
distances to the front ($`s_{tf}`$) and rear ($`s_{tr}`$) vehicles in
the target lane. This shift yielded a modest 4.73% performance
improvement, enhancing interpretability and physical relevance. However,
broader suggestions like game-theoretic logic were not yet implemented,
likely due to their complexity. In the second iteration (V2), TR-Agent
simplified the incentive term ($`I_{incentive}`$) to ($`a_{n}-a_{o}`$),
emphasizing the direct influence of adjacent vehicles, and introduced a
dynamic decision threshold derived from the mean and variance of the ego
vehicle’s speed. These changes led to a substantial performance increase
(47.39%), primarily driven by improved recall, indicating better
detection of true lane-changing instances. Finally, in the third and
most successful iteration, TR-Agent further refined the incentive
formulation using ($`\tilde{a}_{n}-a_{o}`$) and set the decision
threshold to the 75th percentile of the ego vehicle’s acceleration
history. This yielded a significant improvement of 77.68% over the
original MOBIL model, with recall soaring to 0.951. The final model
strikes a strong balance between predictive power and interpretability.

This case study highlights several unique aspects of TR-Agent. Unlike in
the IDM case, not all improvement suggestions are implemented; the Code
Generator selectively prioritizes actionable changes, defers complex
ones, and may reinterpret repeated suggestions creatively. This adaptive
behavior underscores TR-Agent’s flexibility and its potential to mimic
human reasoning in iterative model refinement.

#### 5.2.3 Generalization Studies

To evaluate the generalization ability of the TR-Agent-refined MOBIL
model, we test it on four real-world datasets: three subsets of NGSIM:
Lankershim, Peachtree, and US-101; and the rest is HighD dataset. Note
that we exclude the NGSIM I-80 subset used during model refinement to
ensure fair out-of-distribution evaluation. For each dataset, we
strictly follow the same data construction protocol as in the TR-Agent
evaluation phase.

As shown in
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2.3 Generalization Studies ‣ 5.2 Improvement for MOBIL Lane-Changing Model ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent"),
the TR-Agent-refined MOBIL model achieves consistent and substantial
improvements across all test datasets. The most remarkable gain lies in
recall, which increases dramatically from 0.465 to 0.979 on Peachtree,
0.616 to 0.947 on US-101, and 0.590 to 0.970 on HighD. These results
indicate a substantial reduction in false negatives, highlighting the
model’s enhanced ability to detect true lane-changing intentions. This
capability is especially important for safety-critical applications such
as autonomous driving and traffic simulation. The F1 score, which
balances precision and recall, also improves across the board, exceeding
0.68 on all datasets, with the highest value reaching 0.714 on
Peachtree. This suggests that the refined model maintains a reasonable
trade-off between correctly detecting lane changes and avoiding false
alarms. Although precision remains relatively stable compared to the
baseline, the substantial gains in recall highlight that TR-Agent
focuses on boosting the model’s sensitivity to complex or less obvious
lane-changing behavior. When compared with other classical rule-based
models—Gipps ([Gipps, 1986](#bib.bib19)), LMRS ([Schakel et al.,
2012](#bib.bib45)), and the Game-based model ([Yu et al.,
2018](#bib.bib63))—TR-Agent-refined MOBIL demonstrates competitive or
superior performance. Notably, on HighD, it outperforms Gipps (0.297)
and Game-based (0.505), and slightly surpasses LMRS (0.674) on F1 score,
while retaining interpretability.

These results collectively demonstrate that the improvements made by
TR-Agent are not overfitted to a specific dataset or condition. Instead,
they capture generalizable, interpretable patterns that can be
transferred across diverse traffic environments. This reinforces the
practical value of TR-Agent as a powerful assistant in improving
rule-based models, while preserving clarity and transferability. These
qualities are particularly important in contexts such as transportation
policy development and simulation.

### 5.3 Improvement for LWR Traffic Flow Model

#### 5.3.1 Settings for Model Evaluation

We use the Performance Measurement System (PeMS) ([Performance
Measurement System (varies), PeMS](#bib.bib39)) dataset to evaluate the
performance of the TR-Agent-refined model. The PeMS dataset is a
comprehensive collection of traffic data from California’s freeway
system, providing detailed measurements such as vehicle flow, speed, and
occupancy across various locations and times. Specifically, we use the
PeMS08 data, which is collected by 170 detectors every 5 minutes over 62
consecutive days. During evaluation, we adopt MAE as the primary metric.
To analyze model behavior under different traffic regimes, we divide the
dataset into three traffic density scenarios using a quantile-based
method. That is, we sort selected samples by their traffic density
values and split them into three equally sized groups: low-density
(lower one-third), medium-density (middle one-third), and high-density
(upper one-third). This results in 3339, 1780, and 3942 data points for
the low-, medium-, and high-density groups, respectively. This
percentile-based categorization allows TR-Agent to identify
regime-specific modeling deficiencies and enables targeted refinement,
ultimately improving robustness and generalizability across diverse
traffic conditions.

#### 5.3.2 Improvement Case Study

Figure 10: A complete improvement process of the velocity equation in
the LWR model. On the left are the improved mathematical models and
evaluation results, and on the right are the deficiency analysis and
improvement suggestions. Here $`v`$ is the traffic velocity, $`\rho`$ is
the traffic density, $`v_{f}`$ represents the free-flow traffic
velocity, $`\rho_{m}`$ is the maximum traffic density, and $`k`$ is a
newly introduced hyperparameter to control the steepness of the logistic
curve.

In this experiment, we focus on improving the velocity equation in
Eq.[5](#S4.E5 "In 4.0.3 LWR Traffic Flow Model ‣ 4 Background of Traffic Models ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent"),
which defines the relationship between velocity $`v(\rho)`$ and traffic
density $`\rho`$ as
$`v(\rho)=v_{f}\left(1-\frac{\rho}{\rho_{m}}\right)`$. Unless otherwise
specified, all subsequent references to the LWR model in this paper
refer specifically to this velocity–density equation. As illustrated in
Figure [10](#S5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 5.3.2 Improvement Case Study ‣ 5.3 Improvement for LWR Traffic Flow Model ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent"),
the refinement process is straightforward compared to IDM and MOBIL,
with the model achieving the predefined 50% improvement threshold within
just two iterations. This efficiency is largely due to the simplicity of
the original formulation, which allowed TR-Agent to rapidly converge on
an effective enhancement.

As depicted in
Figure [10](#S5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 5.3.2 Improvement Case Study ‣ 5.3 Improvement for LWR Traffic Flow Model ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent"),
the baseline model adopts a linear velocity–density relationship, which
fails to capture the non-linear nature of real-world traffic flow,
particularly under congested conditions. Performance evaluation revealed
a total MAE of 26.10, with significantly higher error in high-density
scenarios (MAE = 45.12) compared to low-density (6.72) and
medium-density (20.22) regimes. To address this, TR-Agent first proposed
introducing a squared density term to increase non-linearity. However,
this adjustment degraded performance by 5.04%, as it led to overly sharp
speed reductions that did not align with observed traffic patterns.
Subsequent analysis recommended smoother, more flexible formulations,
such as polynomial or logistic functions, to better reflect gradual
changes in vehicle behavior. TR-Agent ultimately adopted a
logistic-based formulation in place of the linear term, allowing for a
non-linear but bounded decrease in speed that better captures real-world
traffic behavior at high densities. This modification introduces a
bounded, continuous decline in speed as density increases, avoiding
unrealistic drops while maintaining interpretability.

The refined model achieved a 92.26% reduction in MAE and delivered
substantial improvements across all density regimes, particularly in
medium- and high-density traffic. This case demonstrates TR-Agent’s
ability to iteratively identify, test, and validate meaningful
structural changes. Even when early modifications fail, the agent
adjusts its approach based on feedback, ultimately converging on robust,
scientifically grounded improvements.

#### 5.3.3 Generalization Studies

real-world test datasets. The number in parentheses indicates the number
of data points used for evaluation in each dataset. All models are
evaluated under low-, mid-, and high-density traffic regimes using MAE.

Building on the promising results observed in the PeMS08 dataset, we
further investigate the generalization capability of the
TR-Agent-refined LWR model across a broader range of traffic
environments. Specifically, we evaluate model performance on six diverse
real-world datasets: PeMS04 ([Performance Measurement System (varies),
PeMS](#bib.bib39)) and five urban datasets—Bolton, Constance, Essen,
Innsbruck, and Rotterdam—selected from the open-source collection
provided by ([Loder et al., 2019](#bib.bib32)), chosen for their higher
data quality and reliability.

As shown in
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3.3 Generalization Studies ‣ 5.3 Improvement for LWR Traffic Flow Model ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent"),
the TR-Agent-refined LWR consistently outperforms the baseline LWR
across all datasets and density regimes. On PeMS04, the average MAE
drops from 4.60 to 2.76, with notable improvements under both low- and
high-density conditions. The gains are even more pronounced in urban
settings: for instance, on Constance, the average MAE is reduced from
14.73 to 7.84, and on Essen from 12.15 to 9.30. These results suggest
that TR-Agent can effectively adapt classical models to varying traffic
complexities, without relying on data-driven retraining. We also compare
the refined model against several established single-regime
alternatives, including Drake’s ([Drake, 1967](#bib.bib15)),
Drew’s ([Drew, 1968](#bib.bib16)), Underwood’s ([Underwood and
Relationships, 1961](#bib.bib54)), and Pipe-Munjal’s ([Pipes,
1966](#bib.bib40); [Munjal and Pipes, 1971](#bib.bib36)). On most
datasets, the TR-Agent-refined LWR achieves lower or comparable MAE,
particularly under high-density conditions. For example, on Constance
and Rotterdam, it outperforms all classical baselines, including those
with nonlinear formulations, demonstrating strong generalization without
sacrificing interpretability.

To better visualize the alignment between model predictions and
empirical traffic data, we overlay the speed–density curves of various
models with observed data on four representative datasets: Constance,
Essen, Innsbruck, and Rotterdam, as shown in
Figure [11](#S5.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 5.3.3 Generalization Studies ‣ 5.3 Improvement for LWR Traffic Flow Model ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent").
Among the models compared, the original LWR adopts a linear
velocity–density relationship. While simple and interpretable, this form
often fails to capture the nonlinear characteristics of real-world
traffic, particularly under high-density conditions. In contrast,
classical models such as Underwood’s and Pipe-Munjal’s introduce
nonlinear functions that better represent observed flow patterns.
Building on the LWR structure, our TR-Agent-refined LWR replaces the
linear formulation with a logistic function, enabling a more accurate
depiction of vehicle behavior in congested regimes, especially the
gradual deceleration of speed as density approaches saturation. As
illustrated in subplots (a), (b), and (d), the refined model closely
follows empirical trends and aligns well with Underwood’s model,
particularly in high-density regions.

![Refer to caption](2409.16876v3/traffic_flow_plot.png)

Figure 11: Visualization of traffic data points and evaluated traffic
model on four selected datasets: (a) Constance, (b) Essen, (c)
Innsbruck, and (d) Rotterdam. Each subplot plots speed against density,
with gray dots representing observed data and colored curves denoting
different models.

It is important to emphasize that the objective of this work is not to
introduce new traffic models, but to demonstrate the effectiveness of a
general-purpose, automated model refinement framework. TR-Agent enhances
traffic model performance through LLM-guided reasoning and structured
feedback, without relying on gradient-based training or direct access to
raw data. While our experiments use IDM, MOBIL, and LWR as
representative baselines, the framework is inherently model-agnostic. We
expect that applying TR-Agent to stronger initial models, such as ACC in
the context of car-following, could lead to more capable and adaptable
traffic models. This further highlights the flexibility, extensibility,
and broad applicability of our approach.

### 5.4 Ablation Study on the Role of Literature Access

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Conditions | IDM Refinement |  |  | MOBIL Refinement |  |  | LWR Refinement |  |  |
|  | NST@20 | AIS | MIR (%) | NST@20 | AIS | MIR (%) | NST@20 | AIS | MIR (%) |
| w/ RAG | 11 | 2.7 | 30.32 | 10 | 4.1 | 77.92 | 15 | 3.5 | 94.16 |
| w/o RAG | 5 | 5.0 | 26.08 | 7 | 5.6 | 81.84 | 9 | 5.2 | 96.8 |

Table 4: Performance comparison of the TR-Agent with and without RAG
module. NST@20 denotes the Number of Successful Trials (out of 20), AIS
represents the Average Iterations for Successful improvement, and MIR is
the Maximum Improvement Rate. The maximum iterations per trial are
limited to 10.

To investigate the impact of external domain knowledge on TR-Agent’s
performance, we conducted an ablation study by disabling the RAG module,
thus restricting the agent to rely solely on its internal pretrained
knowledge.
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.4 Ablation Study on the Role of Literature Access ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent")
presents a comparison across three traffic modeling tasks.

With RAG enabled, TR-Agent consistently achieved higher efficiency, as
reflected by more successful trials within the 20-attempt budget
(NST@20) and fewer average iterations needed for each successful
refinement (AIS). For instance, the number of successful trials
increased from 5 to 11 in IDM and from 9 to 15 in LWR when RAG was
enabled. This highlights the critical role of literature access in
improving search efficiency and guiding the agent toward promising
improvement directions early in the process. However, even without RAG,
TR-Agent still produced competitive results. The maximum improvement
rate (MIR) remains high across all tasks, and in some cases (e.g. MOBIL
and LWR), MIR is even slightly higher without RAG (81.84% vs. 77.92% for
MOBIL; 96.8% vs. 94.16% for LWR). This suggests that when deprived of
structured external guidance, the agent may take a more exploratory or
unconventional approach, occasionally stumbling upon surprisingly
effective refinements. These results also affirm the strength of
TR-Agent’s internal reasoning capabilities and its capacity to improve
models based on self-contained logic and prior training alone.

Taken together, the ablation study demonstrates that while RAG is not
strictly necessary for success, it significantly enhances the
reliability and efficiency of the refinement process. External knowledge
serves as a powerful accelerator, reducing iteration overhead and
increasing trial success rates, especially valuable when refinement
budgets are limited.

### 5.5 Analysis of Performance Trends over Multiple Iterations

Figure 12: The performance trends of the improved models over multiple
iterations: IDM (left), MOBIL (center), and LWR (right). Each colored
line represents a different trial, with improvement rates plotted across
iterations. The black dashed lines indicate the threshold for successful
model improvements. This figure illustrates the variability in
performance improvements across different iterations and trials,
highlighting the dynamic and sometimes volatile nature of model
optimization.

To better understand the dynamic behavior of TR-Agent during iterative
refinement, we visualize the performance improvement trends over 10
successful trials for each model, as shown in
Figure [12](#S5.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 5.5 Analysis of Performance Trends over Multiple Iterations ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent").
The plots display improvement rates across iterations, with the black
dashed line marking the predefined required improvement for a trial to
be considered successful (20% for IDM, 50% for MOBIL and LWR).

For the IDM improvement iterations, most trials experienced performance
fluctuations in the early stages. Several trials, such as Trial 4 and
Trial 7, initially showed substantial drops in performance, with
improvements falling below –80%. These fluctuations reflect an
exploratory phase where TR-Agent tests structural changes that may not
immediately lead to better outcomes. As iterations progress, however,
the agent gradually recovers and consistently exceeds the 20%
improvement threshold, demonstrating its ability to self-correct and
refine its search strategy based on evaluation feedback. In contrast,
the MOBIL task (center) exhibits greater volatility throughout the
entire refinement process. Several trials, such as Trials 5 and 9,
demonstrate large swings between gains and regressions. This instability
likely stems from the complexity of the lane-changing decision logic,
where minor alterations to incentive or safety constraints can result in
disproportionately large behavioral changes. Nevertheless, most
trajectories ultimately surpass the 50% improvement target, underscoring
TR-Agent’s capacity to navigate non-convex and sensitive optimization
landscapes. The LWR task (right) stands in stark contrast. Here,
refinement is much more stable and monotonic, with most trials showing
steady improvements over time. This consistency is likely due to the
simplicity and mathematical smoothness of the LWR velocity equation,
which provides a more predictable gradient of model behavior. Several
trials even achieve near-optimal results (more than 90% improvement),
suggesting that TR-Agent can efficiently converge when the search space
is more structured and less volatile.

Overall, these trends highlight the flexibility and robustness of
TR-Agent. It can handle a range of optimization landscapes, from stable
and structured to highly dynamic and sensitive. Although some early
iterations may result in temporary performance drops, the agent
demonstrates a strong capacity for recovery and convergence. These
observations suggest that TR-Agent not only improves model performance
but also mimics the trial-and-error process of human researchers when
iteratively refining scientific models.

## 6 Discussion

### 6.1 Cost Efficiency of TR-Agent

One of TR-Agent’s most practical strengths lies in its cost efficiency.
Leveraging the GPT-4 API, each refinement iteration incurs an average
cost of approximately \$0.10. Most experiments terminate successfully
within 10 to 20 iterations, leading to a total cost of around \$1–2 per
improved model. In addition to monetary efficiency, the system also
demonstrates strong time efficiency. Depending on the complexity of the
baseline model and the stringency of the improvement threshold, a
successful improvement typically takes between a few minutes and half an
hour to complete. This represents a substantial reduction in both time
and resource demands compared to traditional model development
workflows, which often involve multiple cycles of human-led calibration,
validation, and theoretical analysis. By streamlining this process
through automated reasoning and evaluation, TR-Agent makes model
refinement more accessible and scalable

### 6.2 Ethical Considerations

As TR-Agent automates increasingly complex modeling tasks, questions
arise regarding its role in scientific discovery and its implications
for human researchers. Although the system demonstrates strong
capabilities in generating and refining model structures, it does not
yet possess the capacity for theoretical abstraction or mathematical
derivation. For example, in the LWR improvement case, the final formula
achieved over 90% performance improvement but was not analytically
derived from the original equation
(Eq. [4](#S4.E4 "In 4.0.3 LWR Traffic Flow Model ‣ 4 Background of Traffic Models ‣ Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent")),
leading to potential inconsistencies. This highlights a limitation in
logical continuity, which could lead to interpretability or
generalization concerns. Human intervention remains essential to verify
whether the new model represents a meaningful evolution or merely an
empirical fit.

Furthermore, as the use of AI systems like TR-Agent becomes more
widespread, issues related to transparency, accountability, and trust in
automated research will become increasingly relevant. TR-Agent currently
requires human oversight to assess the scientific soundness of the
generated models and to ensure that ethical considerations are upheld.
Looking ahead, it will be crucial to strike an appropriate balance
between automated exploration and human validation, especially if AI
agents begin to participate in more autonomous scientific theorization.

### 6.3 Limitations of TR-Agent

Despite the strong empirical performance of TR-Agent, several notable
limitations warrant discussion. First, the generalization ability of the
refined models remains constrained by the diversity of evaluation
datasets. As the current experiments rely predominantly on publicly
available data, which tend to be limited in scale, heterogeneity, and
geographic variation, the refined models may not perform consistently
under more diverse or complex traffic environments. This limitation
underscores the need for more varied and context-specific datasets to
better test the robustness of the proposed refinements. Second, the
Evaluator module relies on fixed, manually defined evaluation metrics,
which limits flexibility. While this approach ensures consistency across
trials, it may fall short in capturing nuanced or evolving task
requirements, such as shifting priorities from accuracy to
sustainability, fairness, or comfort. Adapting the evaluation criteria
currently requires manual redesign, posing a bottleneck to broader
applicability in dynamic or multi-objective settings. Third, TR-Agent’s
capabilities are fundamentally constrained by the underlying language
model. While the use of GPT-4 offers strong general reasoning ability
and coding competence, occasional failures still occur, such as the
generation of syntactically correct but non-functional code. These
limitations are likely to worsen with less powerful LLMs. Finally,
TR-Agent currently operates within a unimodal paradigm. It lacks the
ability to process and interpret visual data such as graphs and
diagrams. These modalities are often crucial in scientific modeling,
particularly in domains like traffic, physics, or biology. This
restricts its capacity to engage with the full range of information
commonly used by human researchers.

### 6.4 Future Works

Addressing the above limitations opens several promising directions for
enhancing TR-Agent. A key improvement involves expanding the diversity
and coverage of evaluation datasets. By integrating simulation
environments or synthetic data generators, TR-Agent could evaluate
refined models under a broader set of scenarios, including rare edge
cases or highly localized conditions. Such diversity would provide a
stronger test of model robustness and generalizability. Another
important direction is the development of adaptive evaluation
mechanisms. Embedding LLM-driven logic within the Evaluator would allow
dynamic adjustment of evaluation criteria based on user intent, model
type, or downstream application. This enhancement would make TR-Agent
more flexible and capable of supporting multi-objective optimization, a
common requirement in practical deployments.

To overcome the current unimodal constraint, future versions of TR-Agent
could incorporate visual language models (VLMs) ([Zhang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib64)) to support interpretation of figures, diagrams, and
heatmaps. This integration would allow TR-Agent to reason over
multi-modal data representations, expanding its analytical capabilities
and enabling more comprehensive model assessments. Lastly, although the
current work focuses on traffic models, the architecture of TR-Agent is
domain-agnostic. With appropriate domain prompts and evaluation logic,
the framework can be applied to fields such as chemistry, biology,
finance, and physics. To facilitate this, we have released TR-Agent as
an open-source tool, encouraging its adoption and customization across
scientific disciplines. These extensions could help accelerate
domain-specific model innovation and democratize access to automated
model refinement tools.

## 7 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced TR-Agent, a general-purpose framework for
refining interpretable traffic models through LLM-guided reasoning and
structured feedback. By integrating modular components for idea
generation, code synthesis, evaluation, and performance analysis,
TR-Agent emulates a human-like, closed-loop research process. Through
comprehensive experiments on three canonical traffic modeling tasks, we
demonstrated that TR-Agent consistently achieves substantial performance
gains while maintaining interpretability and domain relevance.
Generalization studies across diverse real-world datasets further
confirm the framework’s robustness and transferability. Beyond
effectiveness, TR-Agent offers practical advantages: it is cost- and
time-efficient, supports explainable iteration-by-iteration reasoning,
and requires only minimal human intervention. Its domain-agnostic design
also makes it readily extensible to other scientific modeling tasks. To
foster broader adoption and community contributions, we have
open-sourced the TR-Agent framework. We believe it offers a scalable and
transparent approach to LLM-driven model refinement and provides a
foundation for future research across disciplines.
````
